Imagine you are standing in a quiet mountain village, deep in winter snow.
Above you, the Sun is ninety-three million miles away.
Just far enough.
Now imagine that Earth slowly begins to drift closer to it.
Sunlight grows with the square of the distance.
Move only ten percent closer, and you get almost a quarter more sunlight.
The Sun looks a little bigger.
A little whiter.
The snow on the roofs starts to slide.
Glaciers melt into rivers.
Lakes rise.
And warmer air holds more water vapor, a greenhouse gas that traps even more heat.
At seventy-five million miles, Earth would get half again as much sunlight as today.
Forests dry out.
Fires start on the hills.
Venus is only about a quarter closer to the Sun than we are.
Its surface is hot enough to melt lead.
We live in a narrow band around our star.
Not too hot.
Not too cold.
